1.explanation: The bug lives entirely in the Shell-session grammar (components/prism-shell-session.js). The top-level “command” token is defined by a RegExp that always starts with either `$` or `#` (i.e. the shell prompt), and then the very first character is re-tokenized as “shell-symbol.” Because this pattern runs on every line, any `#` anywhere in the line—including URL anchors—matches as a prompt and is marked as a shell symbol. To fix this, the grammar must be tightened so that only real prompt characters at the start of a command line (not `#` inside URLs or comments) are captured as shell symbols.
1.bug_scenario: On Prism’s test-drive page with Shell session highlighting enabled, any “#” in the input is being picked up as a shell prompt symbol. In the screenshot you can see the URL fragment “#pre-1-0-9-manifest-spoofing-vulnerability” in the middle of a code block is wrongly colored as a shell prompt (‘shell-symbol’) instead of being left plain text.

2.explanation: The bug resides in the shell-session language definition. The top‐level Prism.languages['shell-session'] grammar (in both the unminified and minified files) declares a “command” pattern that begins with either '$' or '#' and then marks that first character as a 'shell-symbol'. As a result, any line that starts with '#'—even if it’s meant to be a comment inside the snippet—is misidentified as a shell prompt. To fix this, the ‘command’ pattern (and its sub-pattern 'shell-symbol') must be adjusted so that real comments (e.g. lines matching the bash comment syntax) are not captured as prompt symbols.
2.bug_scenario: In the Prism test‐drive screenshot with “Shell session” selected, lines in the code snippet that begin with “#” (intended as comments inside the shell snippet) are being highlighted as if “#” were the prompt symbol. In other words, Prism’s shell‐session grammar is treating every leading “#” as the prompt rather than as a comment delimiter, resulting in incorrect tokenization and highlighting of comment lines.
